name: pbc
why: A pairing-based cryptography library from Stanford, a glimpse into bilinear maps, though it is a library at heart.

brief.what_it_is: PBC (Pairing-Based Cryptography) is a free C library, built on GMP, that performs the mathematical operations underlying pairing-based cryptosystems. It provides routines for elliptic curve generation, elliptic curve arithmetic, and pairing computation. The homepage describes it as meant to be the backbone for implementations of pairing-based cryptosystems, and it ships example programs for several such systems. The fetched pages do not describe the exact inputs and outputs at the API level.
brief.why_it_exists: The author, Ben Lynn, wrote it as a library so that pairing-based cryptosystems could be built on a common base, with speed and portability as goals. He says the API is abstract enough that a programmer needs only an elementary understanding of pairings, without much elliptic curve or number theory.
brief.how_it_works: PBC sits on top of GMP for big-integer arithmetic and implements curve generation, group arithmetic and the pairing itself in C. The homepage says that thanks to GMP, pairing times are reasonable despite the code being C. The pages I read do not go into deeper mechanism detail; the manual's internals chapter covers Type A through Type I curve internals but I did not open it.
brief.install_notes: PBC requires the GMP library. The download page lists the pbc-1.0.0.tar.gz source tarball, a Windows binary zip compiled with MinGW, and a Visual C++ conversion zip (pbc-0.4.7-vc.zip). It also lists third-party packaging: a Homebrew entry, Ubuntu packages, and a Gentoo overlay. The manual's Installing chapter covers a Simple Makefile and a Quick start, which I did not read. No accounts or hardware are needed.
brief.standout: The author writes his own retrospective on the page and tells readers to use something else today: he recommends MIRACL Core, which he says he used himself, and he contrasts its RFC 9380 hash-to-curve against the ad hoc rejection sampling in his own library. Few libraries openly point users to a successor like this.
brief.status: Quiet. The homepage says the library is 'almost frozen in amber' and is kept alive by volunteer patches. The current release on the download page is pbc-1.0.0, and the manual is revision 1.0.0 dated 2006. I did not see a last-commit date for the git repository, so I cannot say more precisely.
brief.caveats: The author's own homepage recommends a newer library, MIRACL Core, for new work. Hash-to-point uses a rejection sampling routine that the author does not present as standard. The benchmark figures (11ms fastest pairing, 31ms short pairing) are from a 1GHz Pentium III and are historical. The homepage describes the library as free but I did not find an explicit license statement in the pages I read. The examples are demonstrations and the author says more work would be needed before any were practical applications. The manual has a Security issues chapter that I did not read.
quotes: The PBC library is designed to be the backbone of implementations of pairing-based cryptosystems, thus speed and portability are important goals.
I started the PBC library decades ago, for a degree. I also graduated decades ago, and as a result, the library is almost frozen in amber.
Today, I would recommend using a newer library instead, such as MIRACL Core, which I used myself when I last played with pairings.
